title: A 0.024mm2 All-Digital Fractional Output Divider with 257fs Worst-Case Jitter Using Split-DTC-Based Background Calibration
problem: Fractional output dividers (FODs) using digital-to-time converters (DTCs) suffer from PVT variations, gain errors, and integral nonlinearity (INL), degrading jitter performance significantly. Prior calibration methods require additional reference clocks or auxiliary PLLs, increasing area and complexity.
motivation: Modern SoCs demand compact, low-jitter clock generators supporting multiple output frequencies; conventional multi-PLL approaches waste power and area, making DTC-based FODs attractive if jitter can be controlled without auxiliary circuits.
method: A fractional divider uses two paired digital-to-time converters—circuits that convert digital signals into precise timing delays—to generate a divided clock. These converters normally suffer from gain errors (wrong conversion ratio) and integral nonlinearity (INL—where the conversion is inconsistent across different input ranges). The system measures both error types by comparing the two converters against each other during normal operation (a process called background calibration), then automatically adjusts for them in real-time. The result achieves a worst-case jitter of 257 femtoseconds in a chip area of just 0.024 square millimeters.
key_novelty: Using two paired digital-to-time converters to simultaneously calibrate each other's gain and integral nonlinearity errors during normal operation, eliminating the need for external reference circuits.
contributions: 257fs worst-case integrated jitter with <-77dBc spurious tones
Split-DTC background calibration for gain and INL correction
Eliminating reference clock and auxiliary PLL dependencies
primary_theme: compact all-digital fractional divider with split-DTC calibration
